_provenance.subject: ultra-processed foods and health
_provenance.source: Prism public API — research.evidence (one call per angle)
_provenance.note: Counts and shares measured from the data. Effect sizes quoted verbatim and verified against their source. Every lane here is observational; the brief reports the association and flags where certainty is graded low or the lane is thin, rather than asserting causation.

deck: Five health outcomes, one direction of travel: ultra-processed food shows a consistent association with harm — strongest for obesity, diabetes and heart disease — but every lane is observational, and causation is the open question.

angles.claim: ultra-processed food consumption increases the risk of obesity
angles.reading: mostly positive framing, with a substantial cautionary minority
angles.note: the deepest lane by far — 18,869 papers on both sides, with a convincing pooled association, but also the clearest confounding debate: an E-value analysis asks whether the link is causal or confounded, and paediatric evidence is genuinely mixed
evidence: "UPF consumption was associated with an increased risk of obesity (OR = 1.55; 95% CI: 1.36, 1.77; I² = 55%)" (Moradi 2021, dose-response meta-analysis)
"the literature strongly supports ... that dietary patterns high in UPF promote overeating and increase the risk of overweight and obesity" (Juul 2025, Nature Reviews Endocrinology)
a cautionary minority: "a 5% increase in risk of developing obesity (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.99–1.13, p = 0.1321)" — non-significant (Gutierrez-Ortiz 2025)
and in children: "inconclusive and heterogeneous evidence ... most cross-sectional studies reported null associations" (Robles 2024, systematic review)

angles.claim: ultra-processed food consumption increases the risk of type 2 diabetes
angles.reading: a consistent dose-response signal, with no contradicting papers in the read set
angles.note: multiple 2025 meta-analyses converge around a risk ratio of 1.4–1.5 for the highest versus lowest intake, backed by a 13% increase per 10% of UPF in the diet
evidence: "summary RR for T2DM risk was 1.48 (95% CI, 1.36 to 1.61)" (Kim 2025, dose-response meta-analysis)
"for every 10% increase in UPFs intake, there was a 13% increase in risk of developing type 2 diabetes (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.12–1.15, p < 0.001)" (Gutierrez-Ortiz 2025)
"the hazard ratio for T2D comparing extreme quintiles of total UPF intake was 1.46" (Chen 2023, three large U.S. cohorts, Diabetes Care)

angles.claim: ultra-processed food consumption increases the risk of cardiovascular disease
angles.reading: mostly positive framing, with a substantial cautionary minority
angles.note: graded 'convincing' (class I) in a BMJ umbrella review — yet the certainty on that same estimate is rated very low; a strong, consistent association resting on observational cohorts
evidence: "convincing evidence (class I) supported direct associations between greater ultra-processed food exposure and higher risks of incident cardiovascular disease related mortality (risk ratio 1.50, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.63; GRADE = very low)" (Lane 2024, BMJ umbrella review)

"intake of ultra-processed food was associated with a higher risk of overall cardiovascular disease (hazard ratio for an absolute increment of 10% in UPF 1.12, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.20)" (Srour 2019, NutriNet-Santé, BMJ)
"participants with the highest intake of UPF had a 68% greater incidence of CVD (HR = 1.68, 95% CI 1.14–2.48)" (Jalali 2024, Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study)

angles.claim: ultra-processed food consumption increases all-cause mortality
angles.reading: overwhelmingly positive framing, which on a citation-weighted corpus can mean consensus or can mean publication bias
angles.note: a real pooled signal, but a thinner lane (37 papers on both sides) with high heterogeneity (I² = 83%); the brief flags the framing itself as a caution, not just the estimate
evidence: "compared to the lowest, participants with the highest UPF consumption had a 15% increased risk of all-cause mortality (HR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.22; I² = 83.0%)" (Liang 2025, dose-response meta-analysis)

angles.claim: ultra-processed food consumption increases the risk of depression
angles.reading: mixed framing with no dominant lean, but the read documents point one way
angles.note: the newest and smallest lane — a reproducible hazard ratio near 1.10 across a cohort meta-analysis and a target-trial emulation, pointing the same direction as the metabolic outcomes
evidence: "each 10% increase in the dietary share of ultra-processed foods was associated with a 10% increase in the hazard of incident depressive symptoms (HR 1.10; 95% CI 1.07–1.14)" (Werneck 2024, NutriNet Brasil + updated meta-analysis)
"high UPF consumption at time zero was associated with an increased risk of depressive symptoms (RR 1.10; 95% CI 1.04–1.18)" (Mengist 2025, target trial emulation)
"4 cohort studies and 17 cross-sectional studies found that consumption of UPF were positively associated with depression or depressive symptoms" (Tian 2023, systematic review)
